summary.heading: Electric charge and Millikan's experiment
summary.html:
• Two types of charge: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
  • Charge is conserved (the total charge of an isolated system never changes) and quantised (always a whole-number multiple of $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C; electron $-e$, proton $+e$).
  • Millikan's oil-drop experiment: charged oil drops between horizontal plates are held still by adjusting the p.d., so $qE = mg$ and $q = \dfrac{mgd}{V}$. The drop's mass came from its terminal speed with the field off. Every charge was a whole-number multiple of $e$: evidence for quantisation.

summary.heading: Charging and grounding
summary.html:
• Friction: rubbing two different insulators transfers electrons; the two objects get equal and opposite charges.
  • Contact: a charged object touching a neutral conductor shares charge, so both end up with the same sign.
  • Electrostatic induction: a nearby charged object (not touching) makes a conductor's free electrons move and separates the charges. Grounding it briefly, then removing the ground before the charged object, leaves it with charge of the opposite sign.
  • Grounding (earthing): connecting to the Earth, which can take or give electrons with no noticeable change, so a grounded conductor is discharged (fuel tankers, lightning conductors).

summary.heading: Coulomb's law
summary.html:
$$F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} \qquad k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$$
  • $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}$ $\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}$; $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ $\text{C}^{2}\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ (permittivity of free space).
  • Inverse-square, like gravity, but it can attract or repel: a positive answer means repulsion.
  • A charged sphere acts on outside charges as if its charge were at its centre: measure $r$ centre to centre.
  • In a material, replace $\varepsilon_0$ by the material's permittivity $\varepsilon$, which makes the force smaller. Air $\approx \varepsilon_0$; paper about $3\varepsilon_0$; glass about $5$–$10\,\varepsilon_0$; water about $80\,\varepsilon_0$.

summary.heading: Electric field strength and field lines
summary.html:
$$E = \frac{F}{q} \qquad E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}\ \text{(point charge)}$$
  • Electric field strength: the force per unit charge on a small positive test charge. A vector, in $\text{N C}^{-1}$ (= $\text{V m}^{-1}$). A negative charge is pushed opposite to $E$. Fields from several charges add as vectors.
  • Field lines start on positive and end on negative charges, never cross, are closer together where the field is stronger, and meet a conductor's surface at right angles.
  • Patterns to sketch: radial for a point charge; for two opposite charges, lines curve from the positive to the negative charge; for two like charges, the lines push apart and the field is zero at a point between them.
  • Charged conducting sphere: outside, radial, as for a point charge at the centre; inside, $E = 0$ (the charge sits on the outer surface).

summary.heading: Uniform field between parallel plates and the electronvolt
summary.html:
$$E = \frac{V}{d}$$
  • Between parallel plates the field is uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from + to −. A charge feels the same force $qE$ anywhere between them. Near the edges the lines bulge out and the field is weaker (edge effects).
  • Work done on a charge moving through a p.d.: $W = qV$.
  • 1 eV is the energy gained by a particle of charge $e$ accelerated through 1 V: $1\ \text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ J. A particle of charge $2e$ (alpha) through 500 V gains 1000 eV.

summary.heading: Magnetic field lines
summary.html:
• Magnetic fields come from magnets and currents (moving charges). Field lines show the direction a compass north pole points: outside a magnet from N to S; closed loops, never crossing, closer where the field is stronger. $B$ is in tesla (T).
  • ⊙ = out of the page, ⊗ = into the page.
  • Patterns to sketch: bar magnet, long straight wire (concentric circles), flat circular coil, solenoid (like a bar magnet outside, nearly uniform inside).
  • Right-hand grip rule: for a wire, thumb along the conventional current, fingers curl the way the field goes. For a coil or solenoid, fingers follow the current round the loops and the thumb points along the field inside, to the north-pole end (anticlockwise current seen from an end means that end is N).
  • New for 2028 The field of a long straight wire, $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, is now in the data booklet (used in D.3).

summary.heading: Comparing fields
summary.html:
• Gravitational and electric fields are both inverse-square: $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$ and $E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}$, with mass and charge in matching roles.
  • Gravity only attracts; electric forces attract or repel. Electric forces between particles are far stronger, but large objects are usually neutral, so gravity dominates for planets.
  • Magnetic field lines are always closed loops: there are no magnetic monopoles. Magnetic fields come from moving charges (currents) and act on moving charges (D.3) and on magnets.

summary.heading: Electric potential energy and potential
summary.html:
$$E_p = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r} \qquad V_e = \frac{kQ}{r}$$
  • Electric potential energy: the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation. No built-in minus sign: like charges give positive $E_p$, unlike charges negative.
  • Electric potential $V_e$ at a point: the work done per unit charge in bringing a small positive test charge from infinity. A scalar, in volts ($\text{J C}^{-1}$), zero at infinity; positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative one. $E_p = qV_e$.
  • Potentials from several charges add as numbers, each with its sign.

summary.heading: Potential gradient, conducting spheres and equipotentials
summary.html:
$$E = -\frac{\Delta V_e}{\Delta r} \qquad W = q\Delta V_e$$
  • The field points from high to low potential. For a uniform field this gives $E = \frac{V}{d}$.
  • Charged conducting sphere (solid or hollow): inside, $E = 0$ and $V$ is constant, equal to the surface value $\dfrac{kQ}{R}$; outside, $E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}$ and $V = \dfrac{kQ}{r}$.
  • Equipotentials: no work along them; always perpendicular to field lines; closer where the field is stronger.
  • Shapes: point charge or sphere, concentric spheres spreading out with distance; parallel plates, equally spaced planes parallel to the plates; inside a conductor, the whole volume; several point charges (up to four), found by adding potentials, small closed loops near each charge.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Forgetting to square $r$, or measuring from a sphere's surface instead of its centre.
  • Prefixes: $\mu$C $= 10^{-6}$ C, nC $= 10^{-9}$ C.
  • The direction of $E$ is the force on a positive charge; electrons are pushed the other way.
  • Field lines that cross, or that don't meet a conductor at right angles.
  • Saying the parallel-plate field is stronger near one plate (it's uniform).
  • Magnetic lines drawn S to N outside a magnet, or the grip rule done with the left hand.
  • HL Putting a minus sign in $V_e = \frac{kQ}{r}$ (the sign comes from $Q$), or adding potentials as vectors.
  • HL Saying the potential inside a charged conductor is zero: the field is zero; the potential equals the surface value.

Experiments and evidence: Millikan never saw an electron. How does 'every charge is a whole-number multiple of one value' count as evidence that charge comes in lumps?
Give students a list of made-up drop charges and ask them to find the smallest common unit. How many drops would they need before they were convinced?
Models: Faraday's lines of force were dismissed as a drawing aid until Maxwell turned them into equations. When does a picture become a scientific model?
What do field-line diagrams show well, and what can't they show (for example, the field between the lines)?
Patterns and trends: Put $F = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$ and $F = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$ side by side. What matches, and what is different?
Why might the same mathematical pattern turn up in two very different forces? Is it a clue about nature or a coincidence?
Evidence from interpretation: Millikan left out drops he judged unreliable. What would make leaving out data good practice, and what would make it bias?
How do modern scientists make such choices transparent (lab notebooks, pre-registration, sharing raw data)?

oracy.activity: Explain it to a younger student
oracy.html:
Explain it to a younger student (pairs, 6 minutes, then swap roles): one explains; the other plays a curious 12-year-old who keeps asking "why?". Question: "How can a negatively charged rod give a metal sphere on an insulating stand a positive charge without ever touching it?"

  • First, …
  • That happens because …
  • So, putting it together, …

Listen for: the rod repels free electrons to the far side; earthing that side lets them flow away; remove the earth before the rod; the rod keeps all its charge.

Are field lines real?: Show iron filings around a magnet. Are the filings showing lines that exist, or making lines because filings clump into chains?
Can something be useful and not real? Compare field lines with lines of latitude on a map.
When is it acceptable to reject data?: Ask students how they decide to repeat or ignore a reading in their own practicals. Would they always say so in their write-up?
Who checks a scientist's decisions about data: peers, reviewers, later experimenters? Is that enough?
Why do different forces follow the same: Both laws involve spreading out over the surface of a sphere ($4\pi r^2$). Does that geometry explain the inverse square, or just describe it?
If we had chosen to describe forces differently, would the similarity disappear?
Can conventions mislead?: Conventional current flows + to −, but electrons move the other way. What problems could this cause for a student, and why do we keep it?
Name another convention in physics (sign of potential, field direction, positive direction in kinematics). What would change if we flipped it?

videos.title: Charge of an Electron: Millikan's Oil Drop Experiment
videos.use: A clear, step-by-step account of how balancing drops gave the elementary charge. Good preparation before the Millikan worked example, or for students to watch at home.

videos.title: DEMO: Charging by Induction
videos.use: Two touching metal spheres are charged by induction with a charged rod, then separated. Pause at each step and ask students to sketch where the charges are; then compare with the grounding method on the topic page.

videos.title: Avoid electric shock getting out of a car!
videos.use: Charging by friction and discharging in everyday life. A quick hook before discussing grounding.
